summaries.example: Imagine a perfect teacher who always knows what is right and always chooses what is good. Would learning something new make the teacher better? Some philosophers say a perfect God cannot become better or worse. They also ask whether God could notice changing times without changing inside. Different philosophers give different answers.
summaries.summary: This entry examines divine immutability, the view that God cannot gain or lose certain properties. Older philosophers separated essential properties, which help make a thing what it is, from accidental properties, which can change while the thing remains the same. The entry also separates immutability from impassibility, the view that nothing outside God can affect God. Supporters connect immutability with perfect knowledge, perfect goodness, simplicity, and being outside time. Critics argue that God seems to respond to events, know changing times, gain new relationships, or act freely. The entry presents replies to these arguments rather than declaring one side victorious.
key_ideas: Philosophers distinguish between essential properties and properties that can change while a thing remains itself.
Divine immutability says that God does not change in accidental properties.
Immutability and impassibility are different ideas; one does not automatically prove the other.
Some arguments support immutability by connecting God with perfection, complete knowledge, simplicity, or timelessness.
Other arguments point to stories about God responding to events, changing power after creation, or choosing freely.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question affects how people understand perfection, time, knowledge, feelings, freedom, and the relationship between God and the world. It also shows how one word—“change”—can hide several different ideas. Careful distinctions help us understand why thoughtful philosophers can disagree about the same religious claim.

important_terms.definition: A property that is part of what something is. For example, being a triangle is essential to being a triangle.
A property that something can gain or lose without stopping being the same kind of thing.
The idea that God cannot gain or lose accidental properties.
The idea that nothing outside God can affect God or cause God to feel something.

questions_to_think_about: Can something change without becoming better or worse?
Would knowing that time has moved forward require a person to change?
Is being unable to change always a sign of perfection?
Can someone be free if their earlier choices already settle what they will do?

summaries.example: Suppose an omniscient being knows a person’s action tomorrow and later knows that the action is happening today. Has the being’s knowledge changed? One answer says the underlying, tenseless fact—that the action occurs on a particular date—was always known; only its temporal description changed. Another view treats knowledge of the present as knowledge of a changing fact. The disagreement shows why theories of time matter to arguments about immutability.
summaries.summary: The entry analyzes the doctrine of divine immutability (DDI), according to which God cannot gain or lose accidental properties. This qualification matters because classical and medieval philosophers distinguished essential properties from accidental ones, and intrinsic properties from properties fixed by external relations. DDI is not identical to divine impassibility: immutability concerns change, whereas impassibility concerns being affected by what is outside God. The case for DDI draws on divine perfection, omniscience, simplicity, and arguments that connect timeless existence with changelessness. The entry also examines challenges. If God knows which time is present, if Scripture depicts divine regret or decision, if creation changes what God can do, or if free action requires new choice, God may seem mutable. Proposed replies appeal to different theories of truth and time, timeless awareness, distinctions between lost opportunities and lost abilities, and changes in a human nature assumed in the incarnation. The discussion maps the competing arguments without settling them by a single test.
key_ideas: The entry narrows divine immutability: it concerns accidental change, not simply every use of the word “change.” Relations to other beings are generally extrinsic, although historical discussions distinguish kinds of real relations.
Immutability does not entail impassibility. A being might change itself without being externally affected, or remain unchanged while always experiencing an external event.
Arguments for immutability often reason from perfect being: a perfect God cannot improve or deteriorate, and necessary perfection may be thought superior to merely contingent perfection.
Arguments from divine simplicity claim that change requires something to remain and something to become different; a being without parts or accidents therefore cannot change.
The knowledge-and-time debate asks whether an omniscient God must change as the present changes. Responses appeal to tenseless truths, truth relative to perspectives, or timeless knowledge.

Biblical depictions of regret, response, and incarnation, as well as questions about divine power and freedom, generate important objections. Defenders reinterpret these cases or distinguish changes in creation from changes in God.
summaries.why_it_matters: Divine immutability is a case study in how metaphysics and theology interact. It forces questions about what properties are real, whether relations can change one side without changing the other, how omniscience fits with temporal passage, and whether perfection requires being outside time. It also illustrates a broader philosophical method: before deciding whether a doctrine is plausible, clarify the exact kind of change or knowledge at issue.

important_terms.definition: A property that belongs to what a thing is and cannot be lost while that thing continues to exist as that kind of thing.
A nonessential property that a thing may gain or lose while remaining the same thing.
A property determined entirely by an object and its parts, rather than by its relations to external things.
A property that depends on something outside the object, especially a relation to another thing.
The doctrine that God cannot change in accidental properties, including some intrinsic and relational properties.
The doctrine that nothing external can affect God or cause God to undergo a state, especially a negative emotion.
The view that God has no parts and is not composed of properties in the way ordinary things are.
A mode of existence not located within temporal succession; in the entry, timelessness is closely connected with changelessness.

questions_to_think_about: Does a change that is neither an improvement nor a deterioration challenge the argument from perfection?
If a relation changes because a creature changes, must God have changed too?
Can a timeless being know what is happening now without having a changing present?
Does acting freely require making a new choice, or can an earlier choice explain a later action without removing responsibility?

summaries.example: Think about a school calendar. On Monday, you know that the concert will happen Friday. On Friday, you know that the concert is happening. Did you learn a new fact, or did you simply describe the same event from a new place in time? Philosophers use puzzles like this when asking whether God’s knowledge changes as time passes. Some say the event itself is one unchanging fact; others think knowing “it will happen” and knowing “it is happening” involve a real difference.
summaries.summary: This entry studies divine immutability, a doctrine in Western philosophical theology. It says that God cannot gain or lose accidental properties—the kinds of features that can change without destroying a thing’s identity. Some of these properties are intrinsic, while others arise from relations with things outside God. The doctrine is related to, but different from, divine impassibility, which says that outside events cannot affect God. The entry explains why immutability attracted many thinkers. They connected God’s perfection with an inability to improve or deteriorate, and connected divine simplicity and timelessness with the absence of change. The entry then considers objections. God seems to know changing times, respond to human actions in scriptural stories, become related to a created world, and act freely. Defenders answer by distinguishing kinds of truth, describing divine knowledge as timeless, or locating relevant changes in creation or in Christ’s human nature. The issue remains a debate involving competing ideas about time, knowledge, perfection, and agency.
key_ideas: The entry focuses on a specific claim: God cannot undergo accidental change. It does not simply say that every possible sense of change is ruled out.
Immutability and impassibility should not be merged. A being could be unaffected by others but change itself, or remain unchanged while responding in a constant way to events.
Supporters argue that a perfect being cannot become better or worse. Some also connect changelessness with necessary perfection and with the idea that God is timeless.
The doctrine has religious and philosophical roots. Supporters interpret some scriptural descriptions of divine change as metaphorical or explain them through distinctions about God’s nature.
Critics argue from God’s knowledge of the changing present, scriptural stories of regret and decision, changes in divine power after creation, and the demands of free action.
Several replies use theories about eternal truths, time-indexed perspectives, and the difference between losing an opportunity and losing an ability.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because beliefs about God depend partly on larger ideas about change and time. It also teaches a useful lesson in reasoning: an argument may work against one kind of change but not another. Studying both the case for immutability and the objections helps us see how philosophical disagreements are built from definitions, assumptions, and replies.

important_terms.definition: A feature that helps make something the kind of thing it is, such as having three sides for a triangle.
A feature that can be gained or lost while the thing remains the same basic thing.
A feature belonging to a thing through its own nature or parts, not through another thing’s relation to it.
A feature depending on a connection with something else, such as being taller than a classmate.
The doctrine that God does not gain or lose accidental properties.
The doctrine that outside things cannot affect God or make God undergo states such as grief.
The philosophical view that God has no parts and is not made up of changeable accidents.
Existing outside ordinary before-and-after time.

questions_to_think_about: If a person changes from knowing “tomorrow” to knowing “today,” is that a change in knowledge or only a change in description?
Could God feel concern for people without that concern beginning at a particular moment?
Does a perfect being have to be unable to change, or could some changes leave perfection untouched?
What is the difference between being unable to do something and no longer having the opportunity to do it?
